question: Can a model forecast an open-ended, multimodal distribution of long-horizon 2D scene motion from a reference image and sparse query-point motion hints more accurately and much faster than dense video generators by autoregressively diffusing short trajectory increments?

key_findings.claim: Myriad represents future scene dynamics as a causal distribution over sparse point-trajectory increments rather than pixels or dense features.
key_findings.evidence: The joint trajectory distribution is factorized first over time and then over query points within a time step. The transformer predicts each displacement conditioned on the image, all past steps, and earlier points in the current step, then updates positions online with key-value caching.

key_findings.claim: The motion-token design combines object identity, current local context, origin appearance, and observed displacement while sharing a spatiotemporal coordinate system with image tokens.
key_findings.evidence: Each token retrieves DINO image features at the original and current point, Fourier-embeds motion, receives a fresh random unit-sphere trajectory identifier, and uses axial rotary encodings for current position, origin, and time. The random identifiers are intended to scale beyond a learned finite codebook.

anchors.section: 3 Motion Tokens and Shared Spatiotemporal Positional Encoding

key_findings.claim: A fused parallel transformer block materially improves rollout throughput, but the paper isolates speed rather than an accuracy-versus-speed frontier for this change.
key_findings.evidence: Self-attention, image cross-attention, and the FFN share normalization and projections and enter one residual update. Relative to an unfused block, the reported 32-step rollout is about 2 times faster at batch size 4 and about 3.7 times faster at batch size 1; no paired prediction-quality result is reported for the fused/unfused comparison.

key_findings.claim: The pointwise flow-matching posterior is stabilized for heavy-tailed displacement values with a multiscale tanh input cascade.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reports motion excess kurtosis in the hundreds, uses a high-variance Gaussian prior, and concatenates tanh transforms at logarithmically spaced scales. The supplement specifies 512 scales from 0.1 to 100,000 and a 50-step Euler solver by default.

anchors.section: 3 Posterior Parametrization with Flow Matching and Scale Cascade
Supplement A.2 Input Value Scale Cascade and Sampling

key_findings.claim: On OWM at equal five-sample count, Myriad has the lowest reported minADE and is orders of magnitude faster than all five dense video baselines.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports OWM Best-5 minADE 0.029 for Myriad versus 0.037 MAGI-1, 0.039 Wan2.2, 0.051 CogVideo-X 1.5, 0.058 SkyReels V2, and 0.054 SVD 1.1. Throughput is 2,200 samples/minute versus 0.051-0.714 for the dense baselines.

key_findings.claim: The strongest fixed-time accuracy numbers primarily measure hypothesis-search throughput, not an equal-sample comparison of predictive distributions.
key_findings.evidence: Best-within-5min takes the minimum error over however many samples each system can produce. At the reported throughputs Myriad can emit about 11,000 hypotheses in five minutes, while MAGI-1, SkyReels, and SVD emit roughly 1.5, 1.5, and 3.6; Wan and CogVideo are DNF. The one-sided minimum gives no penalty for implausible samples, so 0.013 versus 0.066-0.119 cannot isolate model quality from sample count.

anchors.section: Supplement A.6 Open-World Motion Prediction metrics

key_findings.claim: The primary quantitative task is not image-only forecasting despite the title-level framing.
key_findings.evidence: The benchmark task supplies a short warm-up hint h0 equal to motion over the first two frames x0:2. Dense video models receive extra image frames or video-to-video context and Myriad receives point motion. Image-only behavior is shown qualitatively, but no corresponding no-hint OWM table establishes the headline quantitative claim from a single image alone.

key_findings.claim: The OWM benchmark is a small, curated static-camera coverage test rather than a validated estimate of the full open-world future distribution.
key_findings.evidence: OWM contains 95 Pexels videos, one realized future per scene, durations of 2.5-6.5 seconds, manually chosen moving-object points, and TAPNext pseudo-ground truth. Selection prioritizes structured or kinematically constrained motion and excludes excessively stochastic or disconnected motion. Those choices make minimum error feasible but narrow the claimed open-set uncertainty.

anchors.section: Supplement A.5 Benchmark Construction and A.6 Metrics

key_findings.claim: Direct point output and generated-video baselines are compared through asymmetric observation pipelines.
key_findings.evidence: Myriad emits evaluated trajectories directly, whereas each video baseline first generates pixels and then passes those pixels through TAPNext. Their scores therefore combine video-generation and tracker errors. The paper manually verifies tracker trajectories on real videos but provides no reported generated-video tracker control or oracle-video upper bound on OWM in this version.

key_findings.claim: On constrained physical sets, Myriad is not uniformly best at equal sample count but gains a large advantage under the unequal fixed-time protocol.
key_findings.evidence: PhysicsIQ Best-5 is 0.115 for Myriad, worse than CogVideo-X at 0.100 and only marginally better than Wan2.2 at 0.116; Physion Best-5 is best at 0.048 versus 0.061-0.070. In Best-5min, Myriad reports 0.045 on PhysicsIQ and 0.020 on Physion versus 0.137-0.241 and 0.081-0.147 among finishing dense baselines.

key_findings.claim: Fast counterfactual trajectory rollout enables strong billiards action search in the authors' controlled simulation.
key_findings.evidence: With models trained from scratch on simulator data, Myriad reaches 78% planning accuracy at 496.4 actions/minute, versus 84% for the simulator oracle, 36% for a regression head, 24% for a GMM head, 4% for FPT, and 8-16% for dense trajectory/video diffusion variants.

key_findings.claim: The billiards ablations support short-step autoregression and flow matching, but they do not isolate those choices from compute and training-task changes.
key_findings.evidence: For a 0.5-second rollout, mean best-of-5 endpoint error is 0.00141 at 50 steps of 0.01 seconds, 0.00999 at 10 steps of 0.05 seconds, and 0.02823 in one 0.5-second step. The variants solve different per-step prediction problems and use different numbers of autoregressive/ODE evaluations, so the result supports the combined implementation rather than proving a general necessity of stepwise reasoning.

anchors.section: Supplement B.3 Multi-Step Reasoning / Table D

key_findings.claim: The scale cascade helps, but describing its removal as a severe degradation overstates the reported OWM ablation.
key_findings.evidence: Best-5 error changes from 0.029 with the cascade to 0.033 without it, an absolute difference of 0.004 and about 14% relative. Replacing the flow-matching head with a GMM is the genuinely large degradation, to 0.110.

key_findings.claim: Most flow-head quality arrives by five to ten function evaluations, while the reported main setting pays for 50.
key_findings.evidence: Billiards mean best-of-5 endpoint error falls from 0.00361 at one evaluation to 0.00143 at five and 0.00140 at ten, then only to 0.00138 at 50. The last fivefold increase in head evaluations improves the reported error by about 1.4% relative, so 50 is a quality-first rather than clearly balanced speed choice.

anchors.section: Supplement B.1 Number of Function Evaluations / Table B

key_findings.claim: The claimed uncertainty calibration is qualitative and incomplete.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 12 shows a log-log density plot and fitted line only above roughly one-pixel error, while the text reports a large low-error concentration. No calibration error, coverage curve, likelihood, rank statistic, confidence interval, or held-out comparison is provided, and the posterior standard deviation is compared with error to a single realized future.

key_findings.claim: The zero-shot pedestrian-forecasting transfer result is mixed rather than consistently competitive.
key_findings.evidence: Against in-domain Trajectron++, Myriad Best-of-20 ADE/FDE is slightly better on ETH (0.31/0.80 versus 0.39/0.83) but worse on Hotel (0.17/0.30 versus 0.12/0.19), Zara01 (0.53/1.21 versus 0.15/0.33), and Zara02 (0.40/0.91 versus 0.11/0.25). Missing UCY RGB sequences and manually refit homographies further limit comparability.

key_findings.claim: The training hyperparameters are internally inconsistent.
key_findings.evidence: The main implementation section states AdamW betas (0.9, 0.99), whereas supplementary Table A prints (0.09, 0.99) for all three model variants. This tenfold discrepancy in beta1 prevents exact reproduction without consulting code or the authors.

key_findings.claim: Reprojecting expensive 3D tracks does not improve the primary OWM result.
key_findings.evidence: The 3D-to-2D-track model scores 0.036 Best-5 and 0.020 Best-5min on OWM versus 0.029 and 0.013 for the ordinary TAPNext-trained model, despite being designed to remove camera-motion interference. It is approximately tied on Physion and PhysicsIQ Best-5 but does not dominate.

key_findings.claim: Random trajectory IDs offer a small in-range accuracy gain, while their clearest demonstrated benefit is avoiding a fixed learned slot limit.
key_findings.evidence: At 16 billiards tracks, random spherical IDs improve mean best-of-5 error from 0.00150 without IDs to 0.00141; learned IDs score 0.00149. At 24 tracks, the no-ID model still runs at 0.00277 and random IDs score 0.00263, whereas learned IDs are structurally unavailable. Thus Table C supports flexible cardinality more strongly than a large identity-conditioned accuracy effect, and only on the synthetic billiards setting.

method.core_idea: Encode one reference image once, then autoregressively generate sparse user-selected 2D point displacements with a transformer and a cached pointwise flow-matching head, so computation follows scene dynamics rather than rendering every future pixel.
method.mechanism: At each time and query-point index, a motion token combines origin/current image features, motion, identity, and position/time encodings. A causal transformer produces a compact condition for a flow ODE over the next displacement. The sampled displacement updates the point before the next token is generated; fused attention/FFN projections, KV caching, and cached head conditioning make large hypothesis batches fast.
assumptions: A static reference camera makes future 2D point coordinates an interpretable scene-motion representation.
The queried points are visible and trackable and 2D coordinates are sufficient; occlusion, depth, and visibility are not explicit predicted state variables.
A short first-two-frame motion hint is available in the primary quantitative protocol, despite broader image-only wording.
TAPNext pseudo-labels and tracking of generated videos are accurate enough that their errors do not dominate training or comparison.
Teacher-forced short-step conditionals remain reliable under free-running autoregressive rollout.
Sequential factorization over query points is an adequate model of a set even though permutation invariance is not established.
One observed future and best-of-N minimum distance provide a meaningful proxy for coverage of a multimodal distribution.
The unspecified 10M-video internet training collection does not overlap OWM and is representative of claimed open-set motion.
Wall-clock comparisons across heterogeneous implementations, precisions, output modalities, and tracker postprocessing are sufficiently normalized by the reference H200 protocol.

techniques.role: Breaks long-horizon joint motion into locally predicted displacements and explicit cross-point dependencies.
Labels query tracks without a finite learned codebook and permits limited zero-shot changes in point count.
Provides object identity from the origin and local context from the point's current location.
Aligns image and motion tokens using current position, origin position, and time coordinates.
Shares projections and normalization across self-attention, image cross-attention, and the FFN to reduce kernel launches.
Models a non-Gaussian distribution over each next displacement through an ODE velocity field.
Bounds rare large motions while preserving fine displacement resolution across logarithmic scales.
Separates flow time and transformer conditioning so repeated ODE evaluations reuse projections.
Uses cheap samples to cover one observed trajectory or to choose a billiards action by rollout reward.
Uses a 3D tracker to reproject dynamic-camera training clips into the first camera frame.

limitations: Author-stated: the main formulation assumes a static camera and does not jointly predict ego-motion and scene motion.
Author-stated: pseudo-ground-truth tracks from off-the-shelf trackers transfer their biases and failure modes to training and evaluation.
Reviewer-identified: the primary benchmark supplies motion from two frames, so it does not validate the repeated image-only headline claim.
Reviewer-identified: 95 curated static-camera clips with one realized future cannot establish calibration, diversity, or coverage of an open-world distribution.
Reviewer-identified: minADE is a one-sided best-case metric that improves mechanically with sample count and never penalizes implausible modes.
Reviewer-identified: Best-within-5min compares about 11,000 Myriad samples with roughly one to four completed dense samples and thus conflates representation quality with throughput.
Reviewer-identified: direct point predictions and tracked generated videos have unequal error pipelines.
Reviewer-identified: training-video identities and overlap checks for the unspecified 10M internet clips are not documented, limiting leakage and licensing audits.
Reviewer-identified: teacher forcing leaves exposure-bias and long-horizon error accumulation unmeasured.
Reviewer-identified: sequential within-step point factorization is not shown to be invariant to query ordering.
Reviewer-identified: calibration is asserted from a plot without a numerical calibration statistic or coverage test.
Reviewer-identified: the AdamW beta1 conflict between 0.9 and 0.09 blocks exact reproduction from the paper alone.
Reviewer-identified: the billiards planner is a closed synthetic domain trained separately and does not demonstrate real-world intervention or control.
failure_modes: Moving cameras or changing viewpoints entangle ego-motion with object motion and violate the reference-frame representation.
Occlusion, disocclusion, points leaving frame, depth ambiguity, and tracker loss can corrupt a coordinate-only rollout without an explicit visibility state.
An incorrect first-two-frame hint can steer every later autoregressive step toward the wrong future.
Teacher-forced local errors can compound over long rollouts, especially after contacts or rare events absent from training.
Best-of-N evaluation can reward a diffuse model that emits many implausible trajectories as long as one is close to the single observation.
Changing point order may change samples because the within-step factorization is causal rather than demonstrably permutation equivariant.
Heavy-tailed jumps outside the learned scale range may saturate every tanh feature and erase magnitude information.
Dense coherent phenomena may require many points, eroding the sparse representation's throughput advantage.
Generated-video baselines can be penalized by TAPNext failure even when their rendered motion is plausible.
Real-world action search can fail when 2D trajectories omit forces, depth, uncertainty in actuation, or safety constraints.
reusable_insights: Separate dynamics from appearance when downstream decisions depend mainly on motion; sparse state can buy enormous hypothesis throughput.
Factor a hard long horizon into locally predictable stochastic transitions, but test the gain at matched total compute and with free-running rollouts.
Random continuous identifiers can replace fixed learned entity slots when entity count must extrapolate.
Cache both autoregressive keys/values and diffusion-head conditioning; repeated ODE evaluation otherwise dominates pointwise diffusion.
Multiscale bounded transforms are a practical way to expose tiny and extreme continuous values to one network.
Report equal-N quality separately from fixed-time search efficiency; the two answer different questions.
Distribution evaluation needs both coverage and precision, not only the closest sample to one outcome.
When output modalities differ, quantify the error introduced by the adapter or tracker used to put baselines in a common metric space.
open_questions: How well does Myriad perform on OWM from one image with no motion hint, under the same quantitative protocol?
Can OWM provide multiple independent futures or physics-based admissibility labels so calibration, coverage, and implausible-mode rate can be measured?
Does the accuracy advantage remain at equal end-to-end FLOPs, energy, and sample count with a tracker-oracle control for video baselines?
Can the trajectory distribution be made permutation equivariant while retaining KV-cached decoding and explicit interactions?
How should visibility, depth, camera motion, and uncertainty in point identity be represented without paying the full visual tax?
What is the free-running error growth as horizon, collision count, and query density increase beyond training?
Can the 50 flow evaluations be reduced to five or ten without materially changing OWM and planning results?
Does dynamics-only rollout improve real robot or embodied-agent decisions under actuator and perception uncertainty?
Which AdamW beta1 was actually used, and can the authors release auditable training-data provenance and benchmark de-duplication results?

competitive_landscape.title: What Happens Next? Anticipating Future Motion by Generating Point Trajectories
competitive_landscape.difference: It generates dense scene-wide trajectory grids with latent flow matching, whereas Myriad autoregresses a user-defined sparse set point by point and step by step for much cheaper branching; the dense method more directly tests whole-scene geometry and includes modality-controlled RGB-versus-track ablations.

competitive_landscape.title: What If : Understanding Motion Through Sparse Interactions
competitive_landscape.difference: Flow Poke Transformer models a distribution of local motion conditioned on sparse pokes and predicts the future in one shot; Myriad adds causal short-step rollout, cross-trajectory conditioning, a flow-matching head, and throughput-oriented counterfactual planning.

competitive_landscape.title: Track2Act: Predicting Point Tracks from Internet Videos enables Generalizable Robot Manipulation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Sparse point-track prediction and planning competitor.
competitive_landscape.difference: Track2Act predicts goal-conditioned tracks from web video and converts them to robot actions with a residual control policy; Myriad predicts open-ended stochastic scene motion and uses model-based rollout search, but only demonstrates action choice in simulated billiards.

competitive_landscape.title: Generative Image Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: It predicts dense Fourier-domain motion textures for natural oscillatory dynamics and can render looping video; Myriad predicts arbitrary sparse 2D trajectories as causal increments and targets interactions, open-set videos, and rapid branching rather than periodic motion.

competitive_landscape.title: DINO-Foresight: Looking into the Future with DINO
competitive_landscape.difference: DINO-Foresight autoregressively predicts dense pretrained-VFM feature maps and attaches task heads for future scene understanding, avoiding pixels but retaining dense semantic state; Myriad predicts only selected point coordinates, making massive stochastic branching cheaper but omitting general future-feature tasks.

competitive_landscape.title: DINO-WM: World Models on Pre-trained Visual Features enable Zero-shot Planning
competitive_landscape.difference: DINO-WM predicts dense DINO patch features under action sequences and optimizes actions in six closed environments; Myriad emits interpretable sparse point motion in open-set imagery and samples counterfactual actions cheaply, but lacks comparable multi-environment control evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Diffusion Forcing: Next-token Prediction Meets Full-Sequence Diffusion
competitive_landscape.relationship: Causal diffusion rollout and planning competitor.
competitive_landscape.difference: Diffusion Forcing trains sequence tokens at independent noise levels and supports variable-horizon video/state rollout plus guidance; Myriad uses ordinary teacher-forced causal point increments with a separate flow head and gains speed by avoiding dense sequence tokens.

competitive_landscape.title: iPOKE: Poking a Still Image for Controlled Stochastic Video Synthesis
competitive_landscape.difference: iPOKE maps an initial frame and local poke to diverse dense videos through an invertible kinematics representation; Myriad retains only sparse trajectory dynamics, supports many query points and autoregressive branching, and therefore avoids video rendering cost.

competitive_landscape.title: ProbDiffFlow: An Efficient Learning-Free Framework for Probabilistic Single-Image Optical Flow Estimation
competitive_landscape.difference: ProbDiffFlow synthesizes future frames with a pretrained diffusion model and aggregates optical flow, remaining dense and paying the visual tax; Myriad is trained end to end to directly sample sparse long-horizon tracks and is designed for iterative interactions.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first practical formulation of open-set future dynamics as step-wise inference over sparse point trajectories, an optimized autoregressive diffusion architecture, the OWM benchmark, and accuracy matching or exceeding dense simulators at orders-of-magnitude higher sampling speed.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper combines sparse user-chosen trajectory tokens, within-step cross-point causality, fused transformer projections, cached pointwise flow matching, and a heavy-tail scale cascade. OWM and two physical subsets show 2,200 samples/minute and strong equal-five-sample results; simulated billiards shows 78% planning success. Ablations support flow matching, short steps, random trajectory IDs, and fused-block speed.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The specific combination of user-controlled sparse granularity, causal point-and-time rollout, and high-throughput counterfactual sampling appears distinct from dense trajectory-grid generation, FPT's one-shot sparse motion, and causal dense diffusion. The novelty should be narrowed to that systems combination. The primary numbers require a two-frame motion hint, OWM has only 95 single-future static-camera clips, and fixed-time minADE rewards 11,000-sample search without penalizing implausible modes. Those limitations do not erase the efficiency contribution, but they prevent the evidence from establishing calibrated image-only open-world future distributions or a general planning foundation.

reviewer_notes: Primary review plus an independent secondary verification of all 22 pages of arXiv:2604.09527v1, including every equation, main table, references, supplementary hyperparameter table, ablation, ETH-UCY transfer table, qualitative appendix, and language-model-use statement. PDF page renders were used to disambiguate Tables 1-3 and supplementary Tables A-F. Provenance matches the full-text index exactly. Author-reported findings are separated from reviewer inference and contradiction audits. The strongest audits are the image-only versus two-frame-hint mismatch, curated low-stochasticity benchmark versus broad open-world framing, single-future best-of-N metric, roughly 11,000-versus-1-to-4 sample-count confound in Best-within-5min, asymmetric tracker pipeline, mixed PhysicsIQ/ETH-UCY results, weak numerical calibration evidence, diminishing returns past ten ODE evaluations, small trajectory-ID gains, and the beta1 conflict. Nine competitors were rechecked at exact current arXiv versions on 2026-08-23. No unsupported precision or causal real-world planning claim is inferred from qualitative figures.

Reconfirmed the two-frame-hint versus image-only mismatch, curated low-stochasticity OWM selection, one-realization best-of-N and unequal-sample fixed-time confounds, tracker-pipeline asymmetry, mixed PhysicsIQ and ETH-UCY results, beta1 contradiction, weak calibration evidence, ODE diminishing returns, non-compute-matched step ablation, and limited trajectory-ID effect.
